description: Hey! I’m a CS Master's student specializing in data visualization. For this challenge, I’m building "GaiaPulse", a sleek, interactive Earth System trend and anomaly detection dashboard using Python, Pandas, and Streamlit. My focus is delivering a polished, high-impact MVP with clean statistical visualization and intuitive human-centered UI. Excited to tackle Earth observation data and deliver a top-tier project for the Luxembourg event!
summary: GaiaPulse is an interactive web application that empowers students, researchers, and curious citizens to act as Earth system data detectives. Addressing the NASA Space Apps "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, the tool connects directly to the NASA POWER API (powered by MERRA-2 and satellite observations) to retrieve multi-decade climate time-series data for any location on Earth—from Konstanz and Luxembourg to the Amazon Rainforest and Sahara Desert. Users can select key environmental variables (surface air temperature, precipitation, soil wetness, and solar irradiance), visualize raw annual measurements alongside 5-year rolling averages, and automatically run both Linear Regression and non-parametric Mann-Kendall statistical significance tests. By translating complex scientific datasets into clear rate-of-change metrics, p-value significance badges, and plain-English variable definitions, GaiaPulse makes regional climate trend detection accessible, transparent, and actionable.
details:
What It Does & How It Works: GaiaPulse transforms raw multi-decade NASA Earth observation data into an intuitive, browser-based trend investigation dashboard. Users select an Earth science variable, choose a preset global region or enter custom latitude/longitude coordinates, and define a multi-year timeframe (1985–2025). GaiaPulse queries the NASA POWER API, processes the annual time series, computes a 5-year rolling mean to smooth short-term weather noise, and runs two statistical tests—Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression and the non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test—to calculate the exact annual rate of change (slope) and statistical significance (p < 0.05). Users can also upload custom two-column CSV datasets or export analyzed results.

Benefits & Intended Impact: Designed specifically for high school and college students as well as citizen scientists, GaiaPulse removes the programming barrier to Earth system science. It pairs every metric with plain-English definitions and includes a built-in comparative case study demonstrating how a single global driver (such as warming) can produce opposite regional trends (such as soil drying in continental Europe versus extreme rainfall shifts in tropical belts).

Tools, Languages & Architecture:

  • Live Web App: https://gaiapulse.streamlit.app/
  • Source Code Repository: https://github.com/laman-isg/GaiaPulse
  • Language & Framework: Python, Streamlit (web UI & deployment)
  • Data Processing & Statistics: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy (linregress, normal distribution CDF for Mann-Kendall Z-scores)
  • Visualization: Plotly Graph Objects (interactive zoomable time-series charts)
  • Data Pipeline: Live REST integration with NASA POWER Monthly Point API (plus offline fallback resilience)

Super Intelligence (SI) Transparency Disclosure: Large Language Models (LLMs) were used during development to assist with boilerplate Streamlit UI layout, Mann-Kendall statistical function structuring, and documentation drafting. All code, statistical formulas, API integrations, and outputs were reviewed, tested, and verified by the developer. No NASA logos or branding elements were generated or modified using SI.
projectRefs: Statistical test methods to detect trends in time series data
